beats.text: This is the DECOUPLE workbench, running on measured ENPKG data.
Nothing on this screen is simulated. Extract abundances, parasite inhibition and host-cell toxicity are real screen values.
We load a candidate pair: a methyl xanthone at mass 353, and a rotenoid at mass 393. These are mass-spec annotation candidates, not confirmed structures.
On the left, four explanations compete. After the three starting hits, rotenoid alone holds 39.7 percent, and both together 60.3. The data so far can't separate them.
In the middle are fifty sample profiles, each with the relative abundance of both candidates.
The strongest-first rule would assay a Cnestis palala extract, rich in the rotenoid, because it predicts the biggest response.
DECOUPLE recommends Uncarina decaryi green stems instead. It carries the xanthone, with no detected rotenoid.
If the xanthone drives activity, it should respond near 0.99. If the rotenoid does, near 0.05. That gap is the information.
We reveal the assay.
One reveal returns both readouts: parasite inhibition 0.001, host toxicity 0.022. Inactive.
Rotenoid alone jumps from 39.7 to 99.9 percent. Two assays remain.
The next two recommendations are also xanthone-only extracts. Both come back inactive, and the posterior settles.
With the budget spent, we finalize.
DECOUPLE nominates the rotenoid as the single driver, and its host-toxicity channel says it is not the cytotoxicity driver. The next step is a purified-compound assay.
Compare replays strongest-first on identical archived outcomes. It spends its first assay on another active rotenoid extract, and ends with a shortlist: both, or the rotenoid.
Every step can be exported as a JSON decision trace.
Not every pair ends in a single nomination.
For a simple coumarin and a rotenoid, the evidence points to both. DECOUPLE answers: both contribute, do not fractionate. Isolating either one alone would lose the activity.

For a flavone and a rotenoid, the evidence points to the flavone. But the second channel shows it also drives host-cell toxicity, with probability 0.94. So DECOUPLE vetoes it: cytotoxic, do not isolate.
The Benchmark panel replays 952 simulated episodes across 238 compound pairs.
Spending no assays nominates correctly 10.8 percent of the time. Strongest-first and adaptive contrast are close, at 32.2 and 32.7 percent, and both are right 99.4 percent of the time they nominate.
The set-valued verdict answers 98.9 percent of episodes, and contains the true driver 99.4 percent of the time.
The chemistry is real. The response is simulated. DECOUPLE is built to say exactly that.
